column1: Reconstruct the restless heart: God as the soul's good and its rest (Confessions I.1, X.20–23).
column2:
Aim: only an unchanging good can satisfy the desire for happiness, and that good is God.
Premises: everyone wants to be happy (Conf. X.20.29); to enjoy a thing "is to rest with satisfaction in it for its own sake" (On Christian Doctrine I.4.4); what can be lost gives no secure rest (Conf. IV.8.13); everyone wants truth, so "a happy life is joy in the truth" (Conf. X.23.33); that truth is unchanging (VII.17.23).
Conclusion: only God gives rest: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee" (Conf. I.1.1).
Objections: a desire does not prove its object (Schopenhauer); Arendt: if only God is enjoyed, the neighbour is only used.
Reply: premise 5 rests on Argument 10. Augustine's own: love the friend "in Thee" (IV.9.14). Open.

column1: Reconstruct the pear theft: why do wrong for its own sake? (Confessions II.4–10).
column2:
Aim: the root of sin is the will's own turning, with no outside good drawing it.
Premises: ordinary wrongs aim at a lower good: "not even Catiline himself loved his own villainies" (Conf. II.5.11); he threw the pears to the hogs (II.4.9), so he loved "my fault itself" (II.4.9); but a fault is a lack of order, which cannot attract (II.6.12).
Conclusion: the will moved itself, imitating "a darkened likeness of Thy Omnipotency" (II.6.14).
Objection: he then finds motives (II.6.14, II.9.17), so either the theft aimed at an apparent good or the will chose nothing. The Socratic view in Plato, and Kant, deny that anyone wills evil as evil.
Reply (the literature's): MacDonald: the will loved a shadow of God's freedom. He knew theft was wrong, so ignorance cannot explain it.

column1: Reconstruct the case against Manichaean materialism: God and evil need not be bodies (Confessions V.10, VII.1–5).
column2:
Aim: the Manichaean picture of God and evil as two opposed bodies is incoherent.
Premises: Nebridius's dilemma: if the darkness could harm God, God is corruptible; if not, he had no reason to fight (Conf. VII.2.3). Second: "that which may be corrupted must be inferior to that which cannot" (VII.1.1); a God spread through space would have more of himself in an elephant than in a sparrow (VII.1.2); the mind's act of forming images is not itself an image (VII.1.2).
Conclusion: God need not, and cannot, be a body; "whence is evil?" (VII.5.7) need not assume evil is one.
Objection: Hobbes: "incorporeal substance" signifies nothing, so Augustine found only the limits of imagination.
Reply (the literature's): the dilemma uses only the Manichees' own premise; the power to judge bodies is not measured by size (VII.17.23).

column1: Reconstruct evil as privation of good (Confessions VII.12–16; Enchiridion 10–14; City of God XI.9, XII.3).
column2:
Aim: evil is a lack of good in something good, so a good God made everything without making evil.
Premises: God makes only good (Enchiridion 10); "all which is corrupted is deprived of good" (Conf. VII.12.18); a thing without any good would not exist; so "whatsoever is, is good" (VII.12.18).
Conclusion: evil "is not any substance: for were it a substance, it should be good" (VII.12.18). "For what is that which we call evil but the absence of good?" (Enchiridion 11).
Objections: pain feels positive; Mackie: a good omnipotent God would eliminate evil.
Reply (the literature's): the theory answers the Manichees, not Mackie (Evans); Mackie is met by self-caused wills and a God who "can bring good even out of evil" (Enchiridion 11). Aquinas: privation concerns evil's being, not its feel.

column1: Reconstruct the divided will (Confessions VIII.5, 9–10).
column2:
Aim: one self can will and fail to will in one act; the division comes from habit, not two souls.
Premises: "The mind commands the body, and it obeys instantly; the mind commands itself, and is resisted" (Conf. VIII.9.21); in the will's own case "to will was to do" (VIII.8.20); a whole will needs no command, so the resisting will is partial.
Conclusion: two wills, "for that one of them is not entire" (VIII.9.21), in one self (VIII.10.22). Habit: "a lust served, became custom; and custom not resisted, became necessity" (VIII.5.10).
Objection: Pelagius and Julian: necessity removes responsibility; Ryle: a regress of volitions.
Reply: Augustine's own: "I had come willingly, whither I willed not" (VIII.5.11). The literature's (Wetzel): commands are a figure for a will not unified. Frankfurt's addict is the analogue.

column1: Reconstruct memory and the search for God (Confessions X.8–27).
column2:
Aim: seeking needs partial knowing, and God is found through memory but not in it.
Premises: "nor do I myself comprehend all that I am" (X.8.15); the woman who lost her groat found it because she remembered it (X.18.27); all seek a happy life, so all know it somehow: "Truly we have it, how, I know not" (X.20.29).
Conclusion: the search begins in memory and ends above it: "Where then did I find Thee, that I might learn Thee, but in Thee above me?" (X.26.37).
Objection: Plato's Meno paradox; after Aristotle, knowing under a description suffices, without a hidden store of knowledge of God.
Reply: Augustine grants much. Memory supplies only a standard, the refusal to be deceived (X.23.33), and no creature meets it, since every creature can be lost.

column1: Reconstruct the argument about time and distentio animi (Confessions XI.14–28).
column2:
Aim: what we measure as time is a stretching of the mind.
Premises: past and future do not exist (Conf. XI.14.17); the present divides until no part has length (XI.15.20); yet we measure syllables (XI.26.33); so we measure an impression: "It is in thee, my mind, that I measure times" (XI.27.36).
Conclusion: three presents, memory, sight and expectation (XI.20.26); "time is nothing else than protraction; but of what, I know not; and I marvel, if it be not of the mind itself?" (XI.26.33). "Protraction" renders distentio.
Objections: memory impressions vary, so measuring them presupposes the time measured (Russell: subjectivist); Wittgenstein (Investigations §89–90): a puzzle from a bad picture.
Reply: motion outside the mind is granted (XI.23.29–30). Ricoeur, Husserl: lived time is not clock time. Wittgenstein leaves open how a self holds together across time (XI.29.39).

column1: Reconstruct si fallor, sum: certainty against the sceptics (City of God XI.26; On the Trinity X.10.14; Against the Academicians).
column2:
Aim: some knowledge resists the Academic sceptic: I exist, I know it, and I love it.
Premises: the sceptic asks, "What if you are deceived?"; "For he who is not, cannot be deceived"; so "if I am deceived, by this same token I am" (City of God XI.26); the same holds of knowing and loving.
Conclusion: certainty without fear of "the arguments of the Academicians" (XI.26). Also: "even if he doubts, he lives" (On the Trinity X.10.14); X.10.16 infers the mind is no body.
Objections: Lichtenberg, Russell: the self is a further assumption; the result is too thin; Arnauld's masked-man point against X.10.16.
Reply: the literature's (Matthews): a mistake is someone's. Augustine's own: one case of knowledge refutes the claim that nothing can be known; the mind knowing itself "knows its own substance" (X.10.16).

column1: Reconstruct free will and the origin of evil (On Free Choice I; City of God XII.6–7).
column2:
Aim: God is not the author of the evil people do; it comes from a created will's turning, which has only a deficient cause.
Premises: God causes evils suffered as penalty, not evils done (On Free Choice I.1.1, paraphrased); only the mind's own will can make it serve desire (I.10.20–11.21); the turning is a defect: "it is not efficient, but deficient" (City of God XII.7).
Conclusion: moral evil originates in free will. Two men alike see the same body; one consents, and nothing in their natures explains why (XII.6).
Objections: Mackie: God could have made creatures who always freely choose good; MacDonald, Babcock: an uncaused fall looks like chance.
Reply: the literature's: Plantinga's free will defence. Augustine's own: a will that can stray beats a nature that cannot (On Free Choice III.5.15). Open.

column1: Reconstruct the proof of God from truth (On Free Choice II.3–15).
column2:
Aim: something higher than the human mind, eternal and unchangeable, exists, and it is God.
Premises (paraphrased): existing, living and understanding are certain and ranked (II.3.7); what judges is higher than what it judges; whatever eternal and unchangeable thing is above reason, it or what is above it is God (II.6.14); number and the rules of wisdom are unchanging and common to all minds (II.8.20–10.29); no mind judges truth; all judge by it (II.12.33–34).
Conclusion: truth is God, or something above truth is (II.15.39).
Objections: Kirwan: unchanging truths could be Frege's mindless abstract objects; later Wittgenstein: necessary truths are rules of use.
Reply: Augustine's own: the dilemma needs only something above reason, and the rules of wisdom direct love (II.10.28–29). The literature's: realists say convention cannot explain why rules bind. Live.

column1: Reconstruct foreknowledge and freedom (On Free Choice III.2–4; City of God V.9–10).
column2:
Aim: God's infallible foreknowledge is consistent with our acting freely.
Premises: "One who is not prescient of all future things is not God" (City of God V.9); foreknowledge implies an order of causes, and "human wills are also causes of human actions" (V.9); fatal necessity works whether we will or not; that "when we will, we will by free choice" is harmless (V.10). On Free Choice III: foreknowledge compels no more than memory (paraphrased).
Conclusion: "A man does not therefore sin because God foreknew that he would sin" (V.10).
Objections: Pike: God's past belief is fixed; Rowe: a scope ambiguity; the freedom defended is too weak.
Reply (the literature's): Boethius: God sees all times in one present; Ockham, Plantinga: such past facts are not fixed; Rist, Wetzel: a compatibilist Augustine; Stump dissents.

column1: Reconstruct grace and the will: the case against Pelagius (On Nature and Grace; On Grace and Free Will; To Simplician I.2).
column2:
Aim: fallen humans cannot will the good without unmerited grace, which heals free choice.
Premises: fallen nature "now wants the Physician, because it is not sound" (On Nature and Grace 3.3); the will cannot love the good it sees (Conf. VIII.5.10–12); so grace "is not rendered for any merits, but is given gratis" (On Nature and Grace 4.4).
Conclusion: "It is His own gifts that God crowns, not your merits" (On Grace and Free Will 6.15); free will "is not made void through grace, but is established" (On the Spirit and the Letter 30.52).
Objection: Pelagius: God commands only what we can do; Julian: guilt is not inherited; damning infants is unjust.
Reply: Augustine's own: commands show our need; liberum arbitrium survives, libertas is restored. On infants, no reply his critics accepted.

column1: Reconstruct two loves, two cities, and kingdoms without justice (City of God IV.4, XIV.28, XIX.21, 24).
column2:
Aim: no earthly state has true justice, yet states are real peoples ranked by their loves.
Premises: Cicero defined a people by "a common acknowledgment of right and by a community of interests" (City of God XIX.21); right needs true justice (XIX.21); Rome withheld God his due, so "there never was a Roman republic" (XIX.21); "Justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies?" (IV.4).
Conclusion: a people is bound "by a common agreement as to the objects of their love" (XIX.24); two loves form two cities (XIV.28).
Objections: a slide toward coercion (the Donatists, Letter 93); slavery blamed on sin (XIX.15); Arendt: charity cannot found a public realm.
Reply: Augustine's own: XIX.24 ranks peoples; earthly peace is real (XIX.17). The literature's: Markus against Williams and Milbank. On the Donatists, no good reply.

column1: Reconstruct the case for just war (City of God XIX.7; Against Faustus XXII.74–75).
column2:
Aim: Christians can wage war justly, with just cause, lawful authority and a right disposition, while lamenting it.
Premises: war seeks peace (City of God XIX.12); good men may punish its real evils, such as revengeful cruelty, "in obedience to God or some lawful authority" (Against Faustus XXII.74); the just cause is "the wrong-doing of the opposing party" (City of God XIX.7); non-resistance is inward (Against Faustus XXII.76).
Conclusion: such war can be just; the wise man will still "lament the necessity of just wars" (XIX.7).
Objections: Tertullian, Origen: Christians should not fight; Holmes: inward disposition licenses any killing; the divine-command and obedience clauses are too loose.
Reply (the literature's): Markus: no theory, and just war a misery; Ramsey: love for the attacked neighbour; the command concerned Old Testament wars; Elshtain: the lament restrains.

column1: What is the restless heart (cor inquietum)?
column2: Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee (Conf. I.1.1). The opening sentence of the Confessions states the claim the whole book tests. Every human desire is at bottom a desire for happiness, and "a happy life is joy in the truth" (Conf. X.23.33). Only an unchanging good can give secure rest, because the fear of losing anything else disturbs its possession. The death of a friend in Thagaste taught Augustine this (IV.4–9). He tells his life as a search for rest in things that could not give it. In the image of Book XIII, the restless heart is a weight out of its place (XIII.9.10). Pascal restated the theme in the Pensées. Arendt objected that the scheme makes the neighbour a stop on the way.

column1: What is evil as privation (privatio boni)?
column2: Evil is no substance. It is a lack of good in something itself good. Confessions VII.12.18 argues from corruption: corruption harms, harm is a loss of good, and a thing that lost all its good would cease to exist. So "whatsoever is, is good" (Conf. VII.12.18). The Enchiridion makes this a definition: "For what is that which we call evil but the absence of good?" (Enchiridion 11). A wound is "not a substance, but a defect in the fleshly substance" (Enchiridion 11). Moral evil is a privation in the will, "the perversion of the will, turned aside from Thee" (Conf. VII.16.22). The Latin label comes from later writers. It does not claim that evil is unreal or harmless. Plotinus called matter evil; Augustine calls no nature evil.

column1: What were the Manichaean two principles?
column2: The Manichees answered the question where evil comes from with a second principle. Light and darkness were two opposed substances, and evil was as real as good. Augustine was a Manichaean hearer for about nine years. His error, he says, came from one habit of thought: he could think of nothing that did not take up space. "I conceived two masses, contrary to one another, both unbounded, but the evil narrower, the good more expansive" (Conf. V.10.20). On the myth, God fought the nation of darkness and lost part of his substance, the souls of the light, to it. Nebridius's dilemma: if the darkness could harm God, God is corruptible; if not, why fight (VII.2.3)? The privation theory replaced the second principle. Julian of Eclanum later charged that the condemned mass was Manichaeism again.

column1: What were the books of the Platonists, and what was the ascent?
column2: In Milan in 386 Augustine read "certain books of the Platonists, translated from Greek into Latin" (Conf. VII.9.13), in versions by Marius Victorinus (VIII.2.3). Which books they were is disputed: Paul Henry argued for Plotinus, Willy Theiler for Porphyry, and most scholars assume some of both. They gave him incorporeal being, evil as a lack, and a method of turning inward and upward. Entering his inward self, he saw "above my mind, the Light Unchangeable" (VII.10.16). Rising from bodies to the mind that judges them, he reached "the unchangeable and true Eternity of Truth above my changeable mind" (VII.17.23). He fell back at once, "borne down from Thee by mine own weight" (VII.17.23). The books lacked the Incarnation: "that the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, I read not there" (VII.9.14).

column1: What is the divided will?
column2: In Milan in 386 Augustine was convinced and still could not change his life. "The mind commands the body, and it obeys instantly; the mind commands itself, and is resisted" (Conf. VIII.9.21). A will that wills wholly needs no command, so the resisting will wills only in part, "a maimed and half-divided will" (VIII.8.19). "Thus did my two wills, one new, and the other old, one carnal, the other spiritual, struggle within me" (VIII.5.10). Both belong to one self, against the Manichees' two souls (VIII.10.22–24). The cause is habit: "a lust served, became custom; and custom not resisted, became necessity" (VIII.5.10). The struggle ends in the Milan garden (VIII.12.29), presented as grace. Whether the scene happened as told is disputed: Courcelle read it as largely literary; O'Donnell holds it shaped but not invented.

column1: What is the order of love (ordo amoris)?
column2: The will acts by loving. Love (amor) names every movement of the will toward what it wants. Love directed to God is caritas; love that rests in creatures as ends is cupiditas. "So that it seems to me that it is a brief but true definition of virtue to say, it is the order of love" (City of God XV.22). The just person "neither loves what he ought not to love, nor fails to love what he ought to love, nor loves that more which ought to be loved less" (On Christian Doctrine I.27.28). Sin is love turned the wrong way, and grace turns it back. A people too is defined by what it loves (City of God XIX.24).

column1: What are use and enjoyment (uti/frui)?
column2: For to enjoy a thing is to rest with satisfaction in it for its own sake. To use, on the other hand, is to employ whatever means are at one's disposal to obtain what one desires (On Christian Doctrine I.4.4). Only God is to be enjoyed (frui). Everything else is to be used (uti), that is, loved in relation to God. The image is a traveller who falls in love with the journey and forgets home: "this world must be used, not enjoyed" (I.4.4). Use does not mean exploitation. The worry is that neighbours become means. Nygren read the scheme as self-centred eros, and Arendt as making the world a stop on the way. Augustine speaks of enjoying one another in God (I.33.37). O'Donovan argued that to use means to refer a love to God.

column1: What is the weight of love (pondus)?
column2: In ancient physics every body has a weight (pondus) carrying it to its natural place. Confessions XIII applies this to the soul. "The body by its own weight strives towards its own place." Things out of place are restless; restored to order, they are at rest. "My weight, is my love; thereby am I borne, whithersoever I am borne" (Conf. XIII.9.10). The Latin is pondus meum amor meus. The image joins the system. The restless heart of I.1 is a weight out of place. The ascent of VII.17 fails when he is "borne down from Thee by mine own weight" (VII.17.23). Grace sets the weight in a new direction. A person is defined by what they love, and peace is the rest a weight finds in its place (City of God XIX.13).

column1: What is memory, the "fields and spacious palaces"?
column2: Book X of the Confessions looks for God in Augustine as he is now, and passes beyond the senses: "the fields and spacious palaces of my memory, where are the treasures of innumerable images" (Conf. X.8.12). Memory (memoria) is wider than recall. It holds images of bodies, the liberal arts, which did not come through the senses (X.9.16–12.19), past feelings without their being felt again (X.14.21), and even forgetfulness, a paradox he leaves standing (X.16.24–25). It exceeds self-knowledge: "nor do I myself comprehend all that I am" (X.8.15). Everyone knows the happy life somehow, as joy in the truth. God is found in memory but is not one of its images, and is above it (X.24.35–26.37). This echoes Platonic recollection without a past life, which Augustine rejected.

column1: What is distentio animi?
column2: What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not (Conf. XI.14.17). The past is no longer, the future is not yet, and the present has no length. Yet we measure time. Augustine answers that we measure an impression in the mind. There are three presents: "present of things past, memory; present of things present, sight; present of things future, expectation" (XI.20.26). So "time is nothing else than protraction" (XI.26.33), and Pusey's "protraction" renders distentio, a stretching of the mind. The word also names a scattered life: "my life is but a distraction" (XI.29.39). In the recited psalm (XI.28.38), expectation passes through attention into memory. Husserl and Ricoeur built on the account; Russell called it subjectivist.

column1: What is si fallor, sum?
column2: if I am deceived, I am: Augustine's answer to the Academic sceptics, who held that the wise man assents to nothing. "For he who is not, cannot be deceived"; so "if I am deceived, by this same token I am" (City of God XI.26). The same holds of knowing that I exist and of loving it, a triad read as an image of the Trinity. On the Trinity widens the list: "even if he doubts, he lives" (X.10.14). Earlier forms are in Against the Academicians and On Free Choice II.3.7. The certainty is a counterexample to the claim that nothing can be known, not a foundation for all knowledge. Arnauld noted the parallel with Descartes's cogito in the Fourth Objections (1641). Russell objected that the self is a further assumption.

column1: What is the mental trinity (memory, understanding, will)?
column2: The mind is made in the image of a God who is three persons in one being, so Augustine looks in it for a trinity. On the Trinity IX finds mind, self-knowledge and self-love; Book X refines these into memory, understanding and will. "Since, then, these three, memory, understanding, will, are not three lives, but one life; nor three minds, but one mind; it follows certainly that neither are they three substances, but one substance" (On the Trinity X.11.18). Each contains the others: I remember that I understand and will, and so on. Memory here is the mind's standing presence to itself. The image is perfected only when the mind remembers, understands and loves God (XIV.12.15). It remains an analogy, and Book XV lists where it fails.

column1: What are illumination and the inner teacher?
column2: The mind judges bodies by standards it did not get from bodies, such as unity, equality and number. It knows truths that are the same for every mind, such as that seven and three are ten. It sees them in a light not its own, as the eye sees in sunlight, and the light is God (Soliloquies I.8.15; On the Trinity XII.15.24, paraphrased). The Teacher (389), a dialogue with his son Adeodatus, argues that words alone teach nothing. We learn by consulting the truth within, and the only teacher is Christ, the inner teacher (11.38–14.46). How illumination works is disputed. Gilson: God supplies the certainty of judgments, the senses the content. Nash: knowledge of the forms in God. Schumacher: the mind's God-given power of reasoning. Aquinas identified the light with the agent intellect.

column1: What is faith seeking understanding (crede ut intelligas)?
column2: Augustine read Isaiah 7:9 in the Old Latin, taken from the Septuagint, which makes belief a condition of understanding. He made it a rule of inquiry, often compressed as crede ut intelligas, believe so that you may understand (Sermon 43.7.9; Tractates on John 29.6). "Faith seeks, understanding finds; whence the prophet says, Unless ye believe, you shall not understand" (On the Trinity XV.2.2). Belief comes first, as a pupil believes a teacher before seeing the proof, and understanding is the goal. It is not a ban on reasoning. Augustine had tried the other order: the Manichees promised reason without authority, and their reasons failed. All inquiry begins with trust in parents, teachers and historians (Conf. VI.5.7). Anselm used fides quaerens intellectum as the first title of the Proslogion.

column1: What is original sin?
column2: Augustine read Romans 5:12 in a Latin version saying that all sinned in him (in quo), where the Greek eph' hō is better read because all sinned. So the whole race was present in Adam and shares his guilt as well as his punishment. "Hence the whole mass of the human race is condemned" (City of God XXI.12), the condemned mass. Adam's sin was pride, "the craving for undue exaltation" (XIV.13). Inherited guilt shows itself as concupiscence, desire the will cannot master. The damage is to the will, not to nature as created: fallen nature "now wants the Physician, because it is not sound" (On Nature and Grace 3.3). Free choice remains; freedom is lost. Adam was able not to sin; fallen humanity is not able not to sin. Julian called this Manichaeism again.

column1: What are grace and predestination?
column2: Grace is God's unmerited help that makes the will good and then works with it: in us so that we will, and with us once we will (On Grace and Free Will 17.33). Grace, he says, establishes free will (On the Spirit and the Letter 30.52). If faith itself is a gift, God chooses who will believe (To Simplician I.2, 396). From the condemned mass God chooses some by unmerited grace and leaves the rest to just punishment. "Between grace and predestination there is only this difference, that predestination is the preparation for grace, while grace is the donation itself" (On the Predestination of the Saints 10.19). In Augustine it is not a decree to sin. The Second Council of Orange (529) affirmed grace's priority and rejected predestination to evil.

column1: What are the two cities?
column2: Two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self (City of God XIV.28). The City of God (413–426/7) answered pagans who blamed the Goths' sack of Rome in 410 on the abandonment of the old gods. The heavenly city includes the good angels and the elect, the earthly the fallen angels and the reprobate. On earth they are mixed until the judgment, and no institution coincides with either. Neither is the church or the state, and even the church holds members of both (I.35, XX.9). The pilgrim city uses earthly peace and obeys its laws (XIX.17). Markus read a shared secular space; Williams and Milbank rejected that reading.

column1: What is libido dominandi?
column2: The lust for rule is the earthly city's ruling passion. The Preface to Book I of the City of God says the earthly city, "though it be mistress of the nations, is itself ruled by its lust of rule" (City of God I, Preface). Book XIV repeats the phrase: in the earthly city "the princes and the nations it subdues are ruled by the love of ruling" (XIV.28). In V.12–20 the early Romans curb other vices for love of praise, which later gives way to love of domination. God rewarded their virtue with empire, though it was not true virtue, since it served glory. Against Faustus XXII.74 lists "the lust of power" among the real evils of war. Williams and Milbank take this lust to define the earthly city.

column1: What is peace (tranquillitas ordinis)?
column2: Every creature seeks peace, and even war seeks a peace that suits the victor (City of God XIX.12). XIX.13 defines peace as a ladder of orders, each a well-ordered concord, from body and soul up to the city. At the top: "The peace of all things is the tranquillity of order. Order is the distribution which allots things equal and unequal, each to its own place" (XIX.13). The Latin is tranquillitas ordinis. Political peace is one case of the metaphysical order that weight seeks (Conf. XIII.9.10), and peace is the rest a weight finds in its place. The heavenly city on pilgrimage uses earthly peace without enjoying it as its end. It obeys laws that secure life's necessities so long as they permit the worship of God (XIX.17).

column1: What is Augustine's account of just war?
column2: Augustine wrote no treatise on war. The doctrine comes from passages written for other ends, and it sets three conditions: a just cause, which is the other party's wrong; lawful authority; and a right disposition, aiming at peace. "The real evils in war are love of violence, revengeful cruelty, fierce and implacable enmity, wild resistance, and the lust of power, and such like" (Against Faustus XXII.74). "A great deal depends on the causes for which men undertake wars, and on the authority they have for doing so" (XXII.75). The wise man will "all the rather lament the necessity of just wars, if he remembers that he is a man" (City of God XIX.7). Through Gratian and Aquinas these passages began the just war tradition, though Markus argued they give no theory.
